new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress ('vowel stress') is treated as a phonemic suprasegmental of the vowel: it is contrastive, shown by minimal pairs, and is realized with raised pitch. No positional rule for the word is given; any single-vowel syllable may carry it, and within a two- or three-vowel syllable it falls on the first vowel or on /a/. The authors add that it is of infrequent occurrence (not written in the orthography) and that lenis/fortis syllable stress, length, pitch and glides belong to intonation, left for an unwritten syntax paper.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the analysis is explicitly preliminary. Fn. 7 (p. 412) separates 'lenis and fortis syllable stress, length of vowel, raised pitch, and rising and falling glides' as phonemic in intonation, so the word-level status of the stress contrast is left partly open; p. 407 says stress 'is not written because of [its] infrequent occurrence'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/lexeme level (phoneme inventory with minimal pairs); the intonational stress is explicitly excluded and unanalysed. Kemandoga-valley dialect, male informants aged 15-35, CAMA mission data c. 1953-1957.
new_statements.identity_note: Larson & Larson 1958 describe the Kemandoga-valley dialect (the main Moni area; language called Migani by speakers, Moni by Kapauku/Ekari). Drabbe 1949 describes speech of the village Kügapa (Kugapa), east of Lake Paniai. Both fall under moni1261; Glottolog lists no dialect-level codes (Ethnologue names Awembak as a dialect).

Reading lexical (unpredictable) confirmed. Two transcription corrections against the existing quote, from the print: the pronoun is printed /ui/ (úi) (acute only on the phonetic form, not /uí/ (úí)), and the nut is /koá/ (kʰóa) (phonetic accent over o, not (kʰoá)). The catalog record itself has an empty rule field; this source fills it as contrastive, positionally unpredictable stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress ('vowel stress') is one of two phonemic vowel suprasegmentals, established by minimal pairs and realized with raised pitch on the stressed vowel. No positional word-stress rule is stated: any single-vowel syllable may carry stress, and inside a two- or three-vowel syllable the stress sits on the first vowel or on /a/. The authors call phonemic stress infrequent (p. 407: 'vowel stress and nasalization are not written because of their infrequent occurrence') and place lenis/fortis syllable stress, length, raised pitch and glides in intonation, deferred to a syntax paper that never appeared.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the analysis is explicitly preliminary (two minimal pairs only, 'with at least the two vowels /i/ and /a/'). Fn. 7 separates intonational 'lenis and fortis syllable stress' from phonemic vowel stress and postpones it; the Postscript (p. 407) adds that a juncture phoneme can only be proven once 'intonation stress patterns' are analyzed.
new_statements.identity_note: Larson & Larson 1958 describe the Moni of the Kemandoga valley, 10-70 miles NE of the Wissel Lakes, from male informants aged 15-35; the practical orthography adopted there omits stress. Drabbe 1949 (silent on stress) has Moni data from the village Kügapa east of Lake Paniai. Le Roux 1950 (cross-note only) names Moni speakers of Kàpàkoe and Paniè and remarks that speakers of different clans differed in pronunciation and in stress (p. 794). No work describes a Moni variety other than the language itself.

sources.note: Silent on Moni stress placement. The only relevant sentence is in the Ekari section (§2, p. 423): 'De toon die op een syllabe valt geven we aan met een accent grave.' [The tone that falls on a syllable we indicate with a grave accent]; §14 (p. 429) says Moni vowels are 'the same as in Ekari' and marks some Moni forms with the grave (a-noà, agào, dawa-ga-wào, p. 430) but states no rule. Data from Kügapa village.
